meta: A man holding a red pink against a deep blue ground: the portrait attributed to Michael Sittow, made about 1500.
about: A man holds a red pink with both hands at the lower edge of the picture, his eyes turned to the side against a deep blue ground. The Getty says the flower's meaning is a mystery. The pink was named for the time it blooms, around Pentecost, which the Dutch call Pinkster, and the museum suggests its serrated petals recalled the tongues of flame that fell on the apostles. The portrait is badly damaged. Michael Sittow built his glowing surfaces from many layers of thin paint, and the Getty finds a melancholy in the sitter.

meta: A woman in Renaissance dress holding a book as a saint: Amico Aspertini's painting of about 1510, possibly a portrait.
about: A woman in a dark gown with a white lace neckline holds an open book with metal clasps, her fingers marking the page, and a thin halo arcs behind her veil. The Walters says it may also be a portrait. A noblewoman of Bologna might have asked Amico Aspertini to paint her as a saint, as a sign of religious fervour and the holiness she aspired to. She wears Renaissance dress. She holds the book as the Virgin Mary often does. The museum points to the odd shape of the face and the large hands as Aspertini's eccentric style.

meta: The infant Christ asleep on a white cloth: a painting after Bartolomeo Schedoni, probably by an assistant.
about: Naked and asleep in harsh light, the infant Christ lies on a white cloth, while his mother and Saint Joseph appear tiny in the background. The Walters reads his death-like sleep as a sign of his future Passion and the cloth as a reminder of his shroud. It sees Caravaggio's influence in the tender yet brutal naturalism, although Bartolomeo Schedoni may never have met him. Schedoni often had copies made of his works. The museum thinks this version, one of several, was probably painted by an assistant.

meta: Princess Charlotte, daughter of Francis I: Jean Clouet's portrait of 1522, painted when she was about seven.
about: Charlotte of France wears a red headdress edged with pearls and a black bodice over a white chemise with gold trim. Her sleeves are yellow and gold, and her hands are clasped. She was the daughter of King Francis I. The record says she was about seven years old when Jean Clouet painted this portrait. She died at the age of eight.

meta: A courtesan resting beside a screen in the summer heat: Miyagawa Choshun's hanging scroll of about 1750.
about: A young courtesan lounges in the summer heat and opens her robe at the neck to find some relief. She reclines next to a folding screen painted with a cherry tree in bloom. A shamisen, the traditional Japanese instrument, and a songbook lie conveniently nearby. The Art Institute notes that courtesans were often trained to play as part of their repertoire of entertainments. Her kimono carries a pattern of chrysanthemums.
credit_line: Avery Brundage, Frederick and Nathalie Gookin, Samuel M. Nickerson and Louise Lutz Endowments

meta: The anthropologist Frank Hamilton Cushing, painted by Thomas Hovenden in 1890 in a relaxed seated pose.
about: A man in a brown suit and white collar sits and looks straight at the viewer, his hands in his lap, against a pale and loosely brushed backdrop. Frank Hamilton Cushing was an anthropologist at the Bureau of American Ethnology. He spent several years among the Zuni in the Southwest, studying their language and culture. The Zuni adopted him and made him a member of their secret society, the Priesthood of the Bow. The museum says Thomas Hovenden gave him a casual pose that suggests he might get up and stride out the door.

meta: Grace McCurdy and her daughters Mary Jane and Letitia Grace: Joshua Johnson's family portrait from about 1806, now at the National Gallery of Art.
about: A seated woman in a white dress with lace trim is joined by two girls. One stands behind her wearing a red coral necklace, and the other holds a woven basket of strawberries. The sitters are Grace McCurdy and her daughters Mary Jane and Letitia Grace. The family kept the picture. It passed down through Letitia, who married Richard Henry Douglass, and then through later generations of daughters in Baltimore. It was sold at Phillips in New York in 1982. The Corcoran Gallery of Art bought it the next year, and the National Gallery of Art acquired it in 2014.
credit_line: Corcoran Collection (Museum Purchase through the gifts of William Wilson Corcoran, Elizabeth Donner Norment, Francis Biddle, Erich Cohn, Hardinge Scholle and the William A. Clark Fund, 1983)

meta: Flowers and fruit on a plinth below a framed picture: Eelke Jelles Eelkema's still life of 1815.
about: A stone vase holding a bouquet with fruit and vines stands on a plinth, and a glass, a pineapple and some peaches lie beside it. On the wall behind hangs a painting of a woman with a flower basket who hands a child a wreath. Eelkema signed the picture at lower left. The Rijksmuseum has it on loan from the City of Amsterdam, as part of the bequest of A. van der Hoop.

meta: Cherry blossom and autumn maples with poem slips: Tosa Mitsuoki's pair of screens, made for or given to a shogun's daughter.
about: Slips of poetry called tanzaku hang from the branches of a cherry tree in bloom on the right screen. Its mate shows red and gold maples in autumn. The Art Institute reads the scene as the melancholy hours after the courtiers who admired the foliage and recalled classical poems have gone, with the slips as the only trace of people. Courtiers helped Mitsuoki by writing seasonal verse on the strips, taken from anthologies of the 1100s and 1200s. The screens were either commissioned by or given to Tofukumonin, a daughter of the Tokugawa shogun who married the emperor Gomizunoo.

meta: Irises beside a stream from a story of the 900s: Watanabe Shiko's pair of screens on a gold ground.
about: Blue irises and green leaves rise from a gold ground in clusters that shift diagonally across the panels. The subject comes from a text of the 900s about a young nobleman who travels into the lonely countryside, far from the capital at Heian-kyo. By a small stream he finds its banks covered with blooming irises. The Cleveland Museum of Art says the artist chose to focus on those flowers. Looking at them, the nobleman made a poem about his beloved wife, as familiar as a well-worn robe, and the grief of travelling so far from her.

meta: Fishing boats drawn up on a beach, with women sorting the catch: Wijnand Nuijen's painting of 1835.
about: Fishing boats rest on the sand at the left, and a group of women with baskets gathers at the right. In the middle a man on horseback with a boy rides through the scene. Figures in the foreground sort fish spread out on the beach. Far off on top of a dune stands a lighthouse. The signature at lower right reads W.J.J. Nuyen Bz. f. 1835.

meta: Huibert Gerard Baron Nahuys van Burgst in the uniform of an honorary major general: Bastiaan de Poorter's portrait of 1852.
about: An older man with white hair stands before a landscape, his left hand on the hilt of his sabre. He wears a dark uniform with gold epaulettes, red and gold embroidery on the collar and several orders and medals on his chest. The sitter is Huibert Gerard Baron Nahuys van Burgst, a member of the Council of the Dutch East Indies, and the uniform is that of an honorary major general. Bastiaan de Poorter signed and dated it at lower right in 1852. It is on loan from a private collector.

meta: A girl with a kitten on a patterned rug: John F. Francis's portrait of his only daughter, Mary Elizabeth, from 1840.
about: A young girl with dark ringlets and a white dress sits on a floral-patterned rug and holds a kitten. Behind her stand a column and a sunset landscape. John F. Francis added props such as a straw hat with a scarf to this portrait of his only daughter. The museum says the oval format recalls the miniatures that Americans of the 1800s ordered to keep the memory of loved ones. Mary died in 1856, and by the end of that decade Francis had lost all of his immediate family. He lived another thirty years.

meta: Two allegorical figures and a carefree shepherd: Henry Keller's Wisdom and Destiny, shown at the 1913 Armory Show.
about: A nude woman in a green billowing cloak strides across a barren field under a turbulent sky. A clothed figure in a pith helmet sits on a rock beside a goat. Henry Keller based the painting on an essay by the Belgian writer Maurice Maeterlinck, with two allegorical figures at the right and a carefree shepherd at the left who seems unaware of them. It was shown at the Armory Show of 1913. Its success led to a commission for a 70-foot mural at Cleveland City Hall, but Keller withdrew in anger when asked to paint clothes on the nude figure.
credit_line: Gift of Mrs. Henry A. Everett for the Dorothy Burnham Everett Memorial Collection

meta: The sculptor John Gibson: Margaret Sarah Carpenter's portrait of 1857, shown at the Royal Academy and bought by the National Portrait Gallery.
about: A bearded man sits in a dark jacket with a white cravat and a dark bow tie, resting one hand on the arm of a wooden chair against a warm brown background. He is the sculptor John Gibson, a member of the Royal Academy. Margaret Sarah Carpenter, one of the most prominent female painters in early Victorian Britain, painted him in 1857. The portrait hung in the Royal Academy's summer exhibition that year. The National Portrait Gallery in London bought it in 1867.

meta: Sicilian regional dress from Monreale to Syracuse: Saverio della Gatta's watercolour of costumes, about 1820.
about: A man leads a donkey loaded with baskets of fruit at the left, labelled as a fruit seller of Monreale. In the corner stand a woman with a dog, labelled as a woman of Catania, and a woman and a man with a gun and sword, labelled as people of the Piana dei Greci. At the right a woman stands in front of a seated woman with a child, labelled as women of Syracuse and Palermo. Each figure carries a place name. Saverio della Gatta painted this sheet of regional dress in watercolour and ink.

meta: Christ preaching in a Gothic church nave: Cornelis van Dalem's painting of about 1545, with clergy driving off children.
about: Christ sits and preaches to a crowd in the nave of a Gothic church. Richly dressed townspeople, clergy and children stand on a tiled floor between tall stone columns. In the foreground Catholic clergy chase some of the children away. The pointed arches and tall windows recede toward the choir.

meta: Apollo and Pan compete before King Midas: Hendrik de Clerck's oil on copper of about 1600.
about: Apollo plays a fiddle with Athena beside him. In the centre sits Tmolus, the judge of the contest. Next to him is Midas, with donkey ears, and Pan raises his hand in triumph with his pan pipes. Satyrs and muses watch. The picture was painted in oil on copper and sold at auction in The Hague on 1 May 1742, where the catalogue called it the Judgement of Midas by Clerck, full of statues and detail, and the best he had known by him. It fetched 305 guilders.

meta: Madonna and Child with Saint Anthony Abbot and Saint Sigismund: Neroccio de' Landi's altarpiece of about 1490 to 1495, from Rapolano.
about: The Virgin sits in a dark blue mantle and rose gown, holding the Christ Child between a bearded saint in a black habit, who carries a staff with a bell, and a crowned saint in a pink brocade robe. The panel was recorded on the left altar of the church of the former hospital of San Bartolommeo at Rapolano, near Siena, by 1865. The National Gallery thinks it was probably painted for a different church, because Saint Bartholomew is missing and the panel has been cut and reframed. The Kress Foundation bought it in 1943 and gave it to the museum in 1952.

meta: A young woman in profile in an oval miniature: Ezra Ames's portrait of Mrs. Abraham Van Santvoort of New York.
about: An oval miniature in a gold frame shows a woman in profile facing left. She wears a white high-waisted dress with a ruffled neckline and short sleeves, and her light brown hair is curled and gathered up with a ribbon. The Van Santvoort family of Albany founded the Hudson River Day Line in 1828, a steamship company that ran between New York City and upstate New York. The museum does not yet know anything about the young woman herself.

meta: Wisdom on a cloud with a laurel shield and a lamb: José del Castillo's sketch of about 1770 for a cartoon.
about: A female figure in a plumed helmet and white drapery sits on a cloud, gazing upward and gesturing outward, with a laurel-wreathed shield at her side. Cherubs attend her, one holding an open book, and a sheep rests nearby. This is one of four preparatory sketches for cartoons, the full-size designs from which wall hangings were woven. They belong to the decoration of six overdoors in the conversation room of King Charles III's apartments in the Royal Palace in Madrid. José del Castillo based the figures on allegories that Corrado Giaquinto painted for a similar room at Aranjuez.

meta: Anna van Citters in an oval portrait: Simon Du Bois's painting of about 1690, kept in her family until 1876.
about: A young woman with curled light brown hair wears a dark bodice with a white ruffled neckline, a pearl necklace and a pale sleeve. A brown drape frames her against a dark background. The portrait stayed in the Van Citters family, passing from Caspar van Citters to his heir Jacob in 1734. In 1876 Jhr. Jacob de Witte van Citters left it by bequest to the Nederlandsch Museum voor Geschiedenis en Kunst. It was transferred in 1903.

meta: Niagara Falls with tiny figures at the rim: Alvan Fisher's A General View of the Falls of Niagara, painted about 1820.
about: A wide waterfall spills over a horizontal ledge, with a smaller cataract to the left and mist rising above the falls. Dark evergreens frame the foreground. The Smithsonian American Art Museum says the scene conveys the beauty of Niagara Falls, which quickly became an icon for the new nation. Tiny figures stand at the rim of the cataract on a rocky overlook, and the museum reads their gestures as awe and delight. Alvan Fisher made the painting about 1820.
